claims.claim: Only Oskar nucleates cytoplasmic germ granules.
claims.source: This observation was consistent with how these proteins behave in cytoplasmic germ granules; only Oskar nucleates cytoplasmic germ granules (Ephrussi and Lehmann, 1992; Markussen et al., 1995) and recruits Vasa to granules where the two also physically interact (Breitwieser et al., 1996; Lehmann, 2016).

claims.claim: Oskar recruits Vasa to granules where the two also physically interact.
claims.source: This observation was consistent with how these proteins behave in cytoplasmic germ granules; only Oskar nucleates cytoplasmic germ granules (Ephrussi and Lehmann, 1992; Markussen et al., 1995) and recruits Vasa to granules where the two also physically interact (Breitwieser et al., 1996; Lehmann, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Nuclear germ granules are larger than cytoplasmic germ granules (91797 nm2 vs. 44533 nm2).

claims.claim: Initially, mostly small granules with a diameter of 0.7 ± 0.1 µm were present and were similar in size to cytoplasmic germ granules.
claims.source: Initially, mostly small granules with a diameter of 0.7 ± 0.1 µm were present and were similar in size to cytoplasmic germ granules (Figure 2E,F,Gi; Figure 1—figure supplement 1Bi).

claims.claim: Over time, nuclear granules became more numerous, grew in size and accumulated more protein.

claims.claim: Toward the end of the NC 14, characteristic hollow granules with a diameter of 1.7 ± 0.3 µm appeared.
claims.source: Toward the end of the NC 14, characteristic hollow granules with a diameter of 1.7 ± 0.3 µm appeared (Figure 2F,Gi).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2F,Gi.

claims.claim: Fusion of nuclear germ granules was not observed.
claims.source: As with cytoplasmic germ granules, we could not detect fusion of nuclear germ granules.
claims.evidence: This is a negative observation from live imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Nuclear granules did not result from over-expression of Osk:GFP or Vasa:KuOr.
claims.source: Nuclear granules did not result from over-expression of Osk:GFP or Vasa:KuOr since they have been previously observed in wild-type flies using EM and immunofluorescence (Jones and Macdonald, 2007; Mahowald, 1962; Mahowald et al., 1976).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies that observed nuclear granules in wild-type flies.

claims.claim: Nuclear granules formed only in PGCs.
claims.source: Because nuclear granules formed only in PGCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and were populated by Oskar and Vasa (Figure 2Ci–ii), we termed these condensates 'nuclear germ granules'.
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Nuclear germ granules highly concentrated Osk:GFP and Vasa:KuOr while the surrounding nucleoplasm contained 11 to 14 fold less protein.
claims.source: Nuclear germ granules highly concentrated Osk:GFP and Vasa:KuOr while the surrounding nucleoplasm contained 11 to 14 fold less protein, respectively, similar to the levels found in the somatic nucleoplasm (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2H.

claims.source: Furthermore, FRAP kinetics of the condensed Osk:GFP and Vasa:GFP were similar to those recorded for these two proteins in cytoplasmic germ granules (38.8 ± 0.6% mobile fraction,t1/2 of 13.9 ± 0.6 s and 51.1 ± 0.5%, t1/2 of 8.7 ± 0.7 s, respectively (Figure 2I, Figure 1C, Figure 2—video 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E)), indicating that the biophysical properties of cytoplasmic and nuclear Oskar and Vasa were similar.
claims.evidence: This is supported by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: The biophysical properties of cytoplasmic and nuclear Oskar and Vasa were similar.
claims.source: Furthermore, FRAP kinetics of the condensed Osk:GFP and Vasa:GFP were similar to those recorded for these two proteins in cytoplasmic germ granules (38.8 ± 0.6% mobile fraction,t1/2 of 13.9 ± 0.6 s and 51.1 ± 0.5%, t1/2 of 8.7 ± 0.7 s, respectively (Figure 2I, Figure 1C, Figure 2—video 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E)), indicating that the biophysical properties of cytoplasmic and nuclear Oskar and Vasa were similar.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of FRAP kinetics.

claims.claim: Oskar was shown to specifically bind nanos (nos), polar-granule-component (pgc) and germ-cell-less (gcl) mRNAs using in vitro RNA-binding assays.
claims.source: Using in vitro RNA-binding assays, Oskar was shown to specifically bind nanos (nos), polar-granule-component (pgc) and germ-cell-less (gcl) mRNAs (three highly germ granule-enriched and maternally-deposited mRNAs [Little et al., 2015; Trcek et al., 2015]), while it can also interact with a variety of RNAs with lower affinity (Jeske et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Oskar could directly enrich mRNAs in cytoplasmic germ granules.
claims.source: This finding suggested that Oskar could directly enrich mRNAs in cytoplasmic germ granules, the hubs for post-transcriptional mRNA regulation.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that Oskar binds specific mRNAs.

claims.claim: nos, pgc and gcl mRNAs did not localize to the nucleus or nuclear germ granules.
claims.source: Using single-molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization (smFISH) (Trcek et al., 2015; Trcek et al., 2017) we found that nos, pgc and gcl did not localize to the nucleus or nuclear germ granules (Figure 2Ji,Jii, white arrows; Figure 2—figure supplement 1Fi-vi).
claims.evidence: This is supported by smFISH experiments shown in Figure 2J.

claims.claim: Aub and Tud do not associate with nuclear granules.
claims.source: This and the fact that other cytoplasmic granule components such as Aub and Tud do not associate with nuclear granules (see below, Figure 3—figure supplement 1H) suggest that nuclear germ granules may function differently from cytoplasmic germ granules.
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claims.claim: Nuclear germ granules may function differently from cytoplasmic germ granules.
claims.source: This and the fact that other cytoplasmic granule components such as Aub and Tud do not associate with nuclear granules (see below, Figure 3—figure supplement 1H) suggest that nuclear germ granules may function differently from cytoplasmic germ granules.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that nuclear granules lack certain cytoplasmic granule components and mRNAs.

claims.claim: Nuclear germ granules are round and membraneless structures, populated by Oskar and Vasa.
claims.source: In summary, nuclear germ granules are round and membraneless structures, populated by Oskar and Vasa (Jones and Macdonald, 2007; Mahowald, 1962; Mahowald et al., 1976) and behave like phase transitioned condensates.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement supported by data presented in the manuscript and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Nuclear germ granules behave like phase transitioned condensates.
claims.source: In summary, nuclear germ granules are round and membraneless structures, populated by Oskar and Vasa (Jones and Macdonald, 2007; Mahowald, 1962; Mahowald et al., 1976) and behave like phase transitioned condensates.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement supported by biophysical characterization data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Morphologically, biophysically and at least in part by composition, nuclear germ granules resemble cytoplasmic germ granules.
claims.source: Importantly, morphologically, biophysically and at least in part by composition they resemble cytoplasmic germ granules indicating that the mechanism that drives their formation might be shared.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The mechanism that drives the formation of nuclear and cytoplasmic germ granules might be shared.
claims.source: Importantly, morphologically, biophysically and at least in part by composition they resemble cytoplasmic germ granules indicating that the mechanism that drives their formation might be shared.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the similarities between nuclear and cytoplasmic germ granules.

claims.claim: Depletion of germ granule components such as Oskar and Vasa prevents the assembly of germ granules during oogenesis.
claims.source: Depletion of germ granule components such as Oskar and Vasa prevents the assembly of germ granules during oogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Embryos laid by osk or vas mutant mothers fail to form PGCs.
claims.source: As a result, embryos laid by osk or vas mutant mothers fail to form PGCs (Lehmann and Nüsslein-Volhard, 1986; Thomson and Lasko, 2004; Thomson et al., 2008), precluding the observation of nuclear germ granules.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Short Oskar protein coordinates the assembly of both cytoplasmic and nuclear granule types.
claims.source: Consistent with previous studies, our data show that short Oskar protein coordinates the assembly of both granule types but nuclear and cytoplasmic granules differ in their protein and RNA composition.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Nuclear and cytoplasmic granules differ in their protein and RNA composition.
claims.source: Consistent with previous studies, our data show that short Oskar protein coordinates the assembly of both granule types but nuclear and cytoplasmic granules differ in their protein and RNA composition.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data showing that certain proteins and mRNAs are present in cytoplasmic but not nuclear granules.

claims.claim: Translation of osk mRNA produces two isoforms, long and short, that differ in the first 138 N-terminal aa.
claims.source: Translation of osk mRNA produces two isoforms, long and short (Long Osk, Short Osk, respectively) that differ in the first 138 N-terminal aa (Markussen et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: Only Short, but not Long Osk is necessary and sufficient to instruct the formation of cytoplasmic germ granules.
claims.source: Only Short, but not Long Osk is necessary and sufficient to instruct the formation of cytoplasmic germ granules (Breitwieser et al., 1996; Markussen et al., 1995; Vanzo and Ephrussi, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: When transiently expressed in S2R+ cells, Short Osk tagged at its N-terminus with mCherry organized round, membraneless and often hollow nuclear germ granules.
claims.source: Consistently, when transiently expressed in S2R+ cells, Short Osk tagged at its N-terminus with mCherry (Short mCherry:Osk) organized round, membraneless and often hollow nuclear germ granules, while Long Osk did not (Figure 3A–C Figure 3—figure supplement 1Ai,Aii) (also reported by [Jeske et al., 2017]).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claims.claim: Long Osk did not form nuclear germ granules when transiently expressed in S2R+ cells.
claims.source: Consistently, when transiently expressed in S2R+ cells, Short Osk tagged at its N-terminus with mCherry (Short mCherry:Osk) organized round, membraneless and often hollow nuclear germ granules, while Long Osk did not (Figure 3A–C Figure 3—figure supplement 1Ai,Aii) (also reported by [Jeske et al., 2017]).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Three types of Short mCherry:Osk granules were observed in S2R+ cells that differed in size, protein abundance and morphology: small, hollow, and big and non-hollow.
claims.source: Three types of Short mCherry:Osk granules were observed that differed in size, protein abundance and morphology: small, hollow, and big and non-hollow (Figure 3D–F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3D-F.

claims.claim: The small and hollow granules formed by Short mCherry:Osk in S2R+ cells resembled nuclear germ granules described in PGCs.
claims.source: The former two resembled nuclear germ granules described in PGCs (Figure 2B,Ci) (Jones and Macdonald, 2007; Mahowald, 1962; Mahowald et al., 1976), while the latter were observed only in S2R+ cells.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison based on morphological observations.

claims.claim: The big and non-hollow granules were observed only in S2R+ cells.
claims.source: The former two resembled nuclear germ granules described in PGCs (Figure 2B,Ci) (Jones and Macdonald, 2007; Mahowald, 1962; Mahowald et al., 1976), while the latter were observed only in S2R+ cells.
claims.evidence: This is a negative observation from imaging experiments.

claims.claim: The formation of granules in S2R+ cells depended on Short Osk and not on the mCherry fluorophore or the orientation of the fluorescent tag.
claims.source: Importantly, the formation of these granules depended on Short Osk and not on the mCherry fluorophore or the orientation of the fluorescent tag, as N- and C-terminally-tagged Short Osk formed the same granules (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-D.

claims.claim: Short Osk:mCherry formed nuclear granules in HEK293 cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, the ability of Short Osk to organize into nuclear germ granules was not limited to Drosophila cells; when driven by the EF-1α promoter, Short Osk:mCherry formed nuclear granules in HEK293 cells, a human embryonic kidney cell line devoid of Drosophila proteins (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Short Oskar is able to assemble into nuclear granules in heterologous cell systems independent of other germ plasm proteins.
claims.source: We conclude that Short Oskar is able to assemble into nuclear granules in heterologous cell systems independent of other germ plasm proteins.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that Short Oskar forms nuclear granules in S2R+ and HEK293 cells.

claims.claim: 119 proteins were identified in a Short Osk immunoprecipitation followed by mass spectroscopy.
claims.source: We tested a subset of the 119 proteins that we previously identified in a Short Osk immunoprecipitation followed by mass spectroscopy (Hurd et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Many proteins identified in the Short Osk IP were involved in germ cell development and post-transcriptional gene regulation.
claims.source: A gene ontology (GO) term analysis revealed that many proteins identified were involved in germ cell development and post-transcriptional gene regulation including several newly identified mRNA binding proteins, RNP binding proteins and ATP binding proteins such as RNA helicases (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: When expressed in S2R+ cells, Vasa, Piwi, Aub, DCP1, Khc, and CG5726 were not capable of forming nuclear granules on their own.
claims.source: When expressed in S2R+ cells, none of these proteins was capable of forming nuclear granules on their own (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Vasa:GFP condensed into cytoplasmic granules when expressed alone in S2R+ cells.
claims.source: Vasa:GFP condensed into cytoplasmic granules when expressed alone (Figure 3H), consistent with the observations that Ddx4, a mouse homolog of Vasa, forms round and non-membrane-bound cytoplasmic aggregates both in vivo and in vitro (Nott et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3H and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Co-expression of Vasa:GFP with mCherry:Osk readily stimulated its incorporation into nuclear granules.
claims.source: However, co-expression of Vasa:GFP with mCherry:Osk readily stimulated its incorporation into nuclear granules (Figure 3I,J) (Jeske et al., 2017), where 80.3% of granules were populated by both proteins.
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3I,J.

claims.claim: 80.3% of nuclear granules in S2R+ cells co-expressing Vasa:GFP and mCherry:Osk were populated by both proteins.
claims.source: However, co-expression of Vasa:GFP with mCherry:Osk readily stimulated its incorporation into nuclear granules (Figure 3I,J) (Jeske et al., 2017), where 80.3% of granules were populated by both proteins.
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification of co-localization.

claims.claim: Co-expression of Piwi:GFP with Short mCherry:Osk stimulated its incorporation into nuclear granules.
claims.source: Co-expression of Piwi:GFP with Short mCherry:Osk also stimulated its incorporation into nuclear granules (Figure 3J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G), while in the embryo Piwi accumulated in the nuclei of both somatic and germ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3J.

claims.claim: Aub never relocated with Short Osk into the nuclei of S2R+ cells.
claims.source: In contrast, Aub despite its co-localization with Osk and Vasa in cytoplasmic germ granules (Trcek et al., 2015) never relocated with Short Osk into the nuclei of either S2R+ cells (Figure 3J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G) consistent with its behavior in PGCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H), as previously observed (Jones and Macdonald, 2007) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3J.

claims.claim: CG5726 and DCP1 formed distinct round-shaped cytoplasmic granules in the absence of Short Osk.
claims.source: Finally, while unable to form nuclear granules alone or when co-expressed with Short Osk, CG5726 and DCP1 formed distinct round-shaped cytoplasmic granules in the absence of Short Osk (Figure 3J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claims.claim: DCP1 is a core component of the yeast and mammalian P bodies where it regulates mRNA stability through mRNA decapping.
claims.source: While the function of CG5726 is unknown, the biology of DCP1 is very well understood and this behavior of DCP1 is consistent with observations in other organisms and systems; DCP1 is a core component of the yeast and mammalian P bodies where it regulates mRNA stability through mRNA decapping (Beelman et al., 1996; Decker and Parker, 2012), it also affects localization of oskar mRNA in the oocyte and populates Drosophila sponge bodies (Lin et al., 2006), mouse chromatoid bodies (Kotaja et al., 2006) the perinuclear nuage of mouse spermatocytes (Aravin et al., 2009) and the P granule-associated P bodies in C. elegans (Gallo et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: In S2R+ cells, GFP-tagged DCP1 formed spherical, cytoplasmic granules with a protein-lucid core.
claims.source: Interestingly, in S2R+ cells, GFP-tagged DCP1 formed spherical, cytoplasmic granules with a protein-lucid core (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I) similar to the ones formed by Osk in the embryo and in cell lines (Figure 2Ci, Figure 3A,G) suggesting that the biophysical properties driving the formation of Short Osk and DCP1 granules may be shared between the two proteins.
claims.evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claims.claim: The biophysical properties driving the formation of Short Osk and DCP1 granules may be shared between the two proteins.
claims.source: Interestingly, in S2R+ cells, GFP-tagged DCP1 formed spherical, cytoplasmic granules with a protein-lucid core (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I) similar to the ones formed by Osk in the embryo and in cell lines (Figure 2Ci, Figure 3A,G) suggesting that the biophysical properties driving the formation of Short Osk and DCP1 granules may be shared between the two proteins.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the morphological similarity of granules formed by Short Osk and DCP1.

claims.claim: Short Osk forms nuclear granules in S2R+ and HEK293 cells.

claims.evidence: This is a summary statement supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Cell line-expressed Short Osk recapitulated properties of nuclear granules observed in the embryos such as granule morphology and the ability to organize other germ granule components.
claims.source: Cell line-expressed Short Osk recapitulated properties of nuclear granules observed in the embryos such as granule morphology and the ability to organize other germ granule components.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The S2R+ cell system may provide an excellent model to study the molecular and biophysical properties of nuclear germ granules.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that this system may provide an excellent model to study the molecular and biophysical properties of nuclear germ granules.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the utility of the S2R+ cell system.

claims.claim: Short Osk is insoluble during purification.
claims.source: This is particularly important as Short Osk is insoluble during purification (Yang et al., 2015), which would preclude studying the ability of this protein to phase separate in a test tube (Li et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The majority of the Short mCherry:Osk fluorescence was located in granules rather than in the nucleoplasm in S2R+ cells.
claims.source: Similar to the measurements obtained on nuclear germ granules formed in PGCs (Figure 2H), we found that the majority of the Short mCherry:Osk fluorescence was located in granules rather than in the nucleoplasm (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: As the levels of nuclear Short mCherry:Osk increased, the total number and the number of small nuclear germ granules decreased and the number of hollow and big and non-hollow granules increased.
claims.source: As the levels of nuclear Short mCherry:Osk increased (Figure 4B), the total number and the number of small nuclear germ granules decreased and the number of hollow and big and non-hollow granules increased (Figure 4C), indicating that Short mCherry:Osk granules may fuse.
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4B,C.

claims.claim: Short mCherry:Osk granules may fuse.
claims.source: As the levels of nuclear Short mCherry:Osk increased (Figure 4B), the total number and the number of small nuclear germ granules decreased and the number of hollow and big and non-hollow granules increased (Figure 4C), indicating that Short mCherry:Osk granules may fuse.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that granule number decreases while size increases.

claims.claim: Rapid live cell imaging of transfected S2R+ cells revealed that nuclear germ granules did fuse.
claims.source: Indeed, rapid live cell imaging of transfected S2R+ cells revealed that nuclear germ granules did fuse (Figure 4D, Figure 4—video 1) albeit slower and less frequently than P granules in C. elegans (Figure 4—video 2) (Brangwynne et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Nuclear germ granules in S2R+ cells fused slower and less frequently than P granules in C. elegans.
claims.source: Indeed, rapid live cell imaging of transfected S2R+ cells revealed that nuclear germ granules did fuse (Figure 4D, Figure 4—video 1) albeit slower and less frequently than P granules in C. elegans (Figure 4—video 2) (Brangwynne et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison based on live imaging observations.

claims.claim: 46.8% of nuclear Short mCherry:Osk readily exchanged with the granule environment in S2R+ cells.
claims.source: FRAP experiments revealed that in S2R+ cells 46.8% of nuclear Short mCherry:Osk readily exchanged with the granule environment (Figure 4E,F, Figure 4—video 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 4E,F.

claims.claim: The kinetics of recovery after photobleaching in S2R+ cells were similar to those recorded for Osk:GFP in nuclear and cytoplasmic germ granules in the embryos.
claims.source: The kinetics of recovery after photobleaching were similar to those recorded for Osk:GFP in nuclear and cytoplasmic germ granules in the embryos (Figure 4E,F) and comparable to those recorded for P granule proteins (Brangwynne et al., 2009; Sheth et al., 2010), stress granule proteins (Kedersha et al., 2000), P body proteins (Aizer et al., 2008; Andrei et al., 2005) and Balbiani body proteins (Boke et al., 2016) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of FRAP kinetics across different systems.

claims.claim: When granules were only partially bleached, 75.4% of mCherry:Osk fluorescence exchanged during FRAP.

claims.evidence: This is supported by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The recovery of Oskar protein resulted from internal rearrangement of mCherry:Osk as well as its exchange with the granule environment.

claims.claim: Photoconversion of Dendra2-tagged Short Osk revealed that a fraction of Short Dendra2:Osk readily exchanged among neighboring granules.

claims.claim: In S2R+ cells a fraction of nuclear Short Osk actively condensed into granules and dissolved.
claims.source: Together these results indicate that in S2R+ cells a fraction of nuclear Short Osk actively condensed into granules and dissolved, a behavior similar to cytoplasmic germ granules in the embryo (Figure 1C–D) and to P granules in C. elegans (Brangwynne et al., 2009; Sheth et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on FRAP and photoconversion experiments.

claims.claim: Less than 50 percent of Oskar was mobile in the three types of granules analyzed (cytoplasmic and nuclear germ granules in the embryo and nuclear germ granules in S2R+ cells).
claims.source: Despite the ability to exchange, less than 50 percent of Oskar was mobile in the three types of granules analyzed (cytoplasmic and nuclear germ granules in the embryo and nuclear germ granules in S2R+ cells) (Figure 4E,F), suggesting that Drosophila cytoplasmic and nuclear germ granules appear more stable than other phase separated granules (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of FRAP data from multiple experiments.

claims.claim: Drosophila cytoplasmic and nuclear germ granules appear more stable than other phase separated granules.
claims.source: Despite the ability to exchange, less than 50 percent of Oskar was mobile in the three types of granules analyzed (cytoplasmic and nuclear germ granules in the embryo and nuclear germ granules in S2R+ cells) (Figure 4E,F), suggesting that Drosophila cytoplasmic and nuclear germ granules appear more stable than other phase separated granules (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of FRAP kinetics.

claims.claim: Short Dendra2:Osk granules isolated from S2R+ cells could still be observed one hour after purification.

results.result: Cytoplasmic germ granules in Drosophila are phase transitioned condensates displaying both liquid-like and hydrogel-like properties. Oskar and Vasa proteins are highly concentrated in granules (15-21 fold enrichment), with approximately 43-46% of protein being mobile and exchanging among neighboring granules, while the remainder is stably associated. Unlike C. elegans P granules, Drosophila cytoplasmic germ granules do not fuse.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C53 provide comprehensive biophysical characterization through FRAP, FLIP, and quantitative fluorescence measurements. The data consistently show concentration enrichment, partial protein mobility, and exchange among granules. The comparison to P granules (C52) provides appropriate context. The conclusion that these are phase transitioned condensates (C53) is well-supported by the combination of liquid-like properties (protein exchange) and hydrogel-like properties (immobile fraction, lack of fusion).

results.result: Nuclear germ granules form in PGCs and are phase transitioned condensates populated by Oskar and Vasa. These granules grow in size and number as PGCs develop, with nuclear granules being approximately twice as large as cytoplasmic granules. Vasa requires Oskar for nuclear granule localization, and the biophysical properties of nuclear and cytoplasmic granules are similar.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C73 provide detailed characterization of nuclear germ granules through imaging, quantification, and FRAP analysis. The data show temporal progression of granule formation (C57, C64-C66), size differences (C63), protein concentration (C70), and similar FRAP kinetics to cytoplasmic granules (C71-C73). The observation that Vasa requires Oskar (C59-C60) is supported by negative observations and is consistent with cytoplasmic granule behavior (C61-C62).

results.result: Short Oskar drives nuclear granule formation in heterologous cell systems (S2R+ and HEK293 cells) independent of other germ plasm proteins. The cell line-expressed Short Oskar recapitulates key properties of nuclear granules observed in embryos, including morphology and the ability to recruit other germ granule components.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C96 demonstrate that Short Oskar alone is sufficient to form nuclear granules in both Drosophila S2R+ cells and human HEK293 cells, while Long Oskar does not (C90). The granules formed in cell lines resemble those in embryos (C92, C110), and the system recapitulates essential features (C129). This provides strong evidence for Oskar as the nucleator of nuclear granules and validates the cell culture system as a model.

results.result: Nuclear germ granules in S2R+ cells are phase transitioned condensates with both liquid-like and hydrogel-like properties. Approximately 47% of Short Oskar is mobile and exchanges among granules, while the remainder is stably associated. The granules can fuse, resist dissolution by aliphatic alcohols, and remain stable after purification.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C131 provide comprehensive biophysical characterization of nuclear granules in S2R+ cells through FRAP (C118-C121), photoconversion (C122), fusion analysis (C116-C117), and stability assays (C126-C127). The FRAP kinetics are similar to those in embryos (C119), and the resistance to aliphatic alcohols (C127) supports hydrogel-like properties. The combination of liquid-like behavior (fusion, exchange) and hydrogel-like stability provides strong evidence for phase transitioned condensates.

results.result: Multiple independent Oskar protein domains (LOTUS, L1, L2, SGNH) synergize to promote granule phase separation. No single domain is required for granule formation per se, but each domain affects the efficiency of granule formation. Deletion of individual domains results in more diffusely distributed Oskar that phase separates into granules later than full-length Oskar.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C148 present systematic deletion analysis showing that no single domain is essential for granule formation (C138), but each contributes to efficiency (C146-C147). The data show that truncated versions have more diffuse protein and delayed granule formation (C147), supporting the conclusion of synergistic action (C148). This is consistent with the concept of multivalent interactions in phase separation. However, the functional consequences of domain deletions (e.g., C139, C141) suggest specific roles beyond just phase separation efficiency.

results.result: Deletion of Oskar's nuclear localization sequence (NLS1) specifically ablates nuclear granule formation in both S2R+ cells and embryos. NLS1, located in the L1 region, is the major contributor to nuclear localization of Oskar granules. Deletion of NLS1 does not affect Oskar's ability to form cytoplasmic granules or co-localize with Vasa in the cytoplasm.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C156 provide strong evidence through NLS prediction (C150), deletion analysis in S2R+ cells (C151-C152), and CRISPR-generated embryos (C154-C156). The specificity of the phenotype is demonstrated by the retention of cytoplasmic granule formation (C151, C153) and Vasa co-localization in the cytoplasm (C153). The use of two independent CRISPR alleles (C154) strengthens the conclusion by controlling for off-target effects.

results.result: Nuclear germ granules promote germ cell divisions, thereby increasing PGC number. Deletion of Oskar's NLS results in a statistically significant 39.3% decrease in PGC number at NC14 (from 36.9±1.1 to 22.4±1.2 PGCs, p<0.001). Live imaging reveals that OskΔNLS PGCs divide asynchronously with fewer divisions overall and increased time between divisions, while PGC formation and maintenance appear normal.
results.evaluation: Claims C157-C169 provide robust evidence through fixed embryo quantification (C157-C159) and live imaging (C163-C168). The statistical significance is clearly stated (C159), and appropriate controls show that PGC bud number is unchanged (C160), ruling out defects in nuclear migration. Live imaging demonstrates that the phenotype is specifically due to division defects (C165-C166, C169) rather than cell death or maintenance issues (C168). The conclusion that nuclear Oskar controls PGC division (C181-C182) is well-supported.

results.result: The reduced PGC number in OskΔNLS embryos is not due to changes in germ plasm protein levels or most localized mRNAs. Oskar and Vasa protein levels are similar between genotypes, as are CycB and nos mRNA levels. PGCs remain transcriptionally repressed, and embryo hatching is normal. While gcl mRNA is reduced by 52.6%, this does not account for the phenotype as PGC formation appears normal and gcl overexpression does not rescue.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C178 systematically rule out alternative explanations through Western blotting (C170-C171), smFISH (C172, C175), egg hatching assays (C173), and transcriptional repression analysis (C174). The gcl reduction (C175) is addressed by showing normal PGC formation (C176) and lack of rescue by overexpression (C177). This strengthens the conclusion that the phenotype is due to a novel function of nuclear Oskar in division control (C178) rather than indirect effects on germ plasm composition.

results.result: Nuclear and cytoplasmic germ granules differ in their protein and RNA composition. Nuclear granules lack nos, pgc, and gcl mRNAs, as well as Aubergine and Tudor proteins, suggesting they regulate different aspects of PGC development compared to cytoplasmic granules.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C77 provide direct evidence through smFISH and immunofluorescence showing absence of specific mRNAs and proteins in nuclear granules. The inference that nuclear granules function differently (C78, C184) is reasonable given the compositional differences, though the specific functions remain to be fully elucidated. The data support the conclusion that the two granule types have distinct compositions (C86, C183).

results.result: When expressed in S2R+ cells, core germ plasm proteins (Vasa, Piwi, Aub, DCP1, Khc, CG5726) cannot form nuclear granules on their own. Vasa forms cytoplasmic granules alone but is recruited to nuclear granules when co-expressed with Oskar (80.3% co-localization). Piwi is also recruited to nuclear granules by Oskar, while Aubergine remains cytoplasmic.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C105 demonstrate through systematic co-expression experiments that Oskar is unique in its ability to form nuclear granules. The quantification of co-localization (C102) and the specificity of recruitment (Vasa and Piwi recruited, Aub not) provide strong evidence. The behavior of Vasa (C100-C101) is consistent with its known properties and supports the conclusion that Oskar is the nucleator.

results.result: Mass spectrometry of Short Oskar immunoprecipitates identified 119 proteins involved in germ cell development and post-transcriptional gene regulation. Several cell cycle components (Mcm3, Mcm5, Dpa, Apc7, Cdc16) were enriched, and mcm5 and mcm3 mRNAs are posteriorly localized.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 describe the mass spectrometry results with GO term analysis supporting functional enrichment. Claims C190-C191 highlight specific cell cycle proteins that could be relevant to the division phenotype. However, the presence of proteins in an IP does not necessarily mean they are functional components of granules in vivo. The mRNA localization data (C191) provides additional support but does not establish a mechanistic link to the division phenotype.

results.result: Expression of Short Oskar in S2R+ cells does not affect their ability to divide, indicating that the regulatory function of nuclear germ granules on cell division is restricted to PGCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C179-C180 provide cell cycle analysis data showing that S2R+ cells expressing Short Oskar divide normally. This supports the conclusion that the division regulation is PGC-specific (C180). However, this could also reflect the absence of PGC-specific factors in S2R+ cells rather than an intrinsic property of the granules. The interpretation is reasonable but alternative explanations exist.

results.result: Oskar protein is essential for germ plasm formation and nucleates both cytoplasmic and nuclear germ granules. Short Oskar recruits other germ plasm components including Vasa, Tudor, and Aubergine, while Long Oskar is involved in actin meshwork formation and granule tethering. Only Short Oskar is necessary and sufficient for cytoplasmic germ granule formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C27, C61-C62, C83-C85, C87-C88 summarize well-established knowledge in the field supported by multiple citations. Claim C195 extends this to nuclear granules based on the current study's data. This provides essential background context and is well-supported by the literature and current findings.

results.result: Several speculative models are proposed for how nuclear germ granules might regulate PGC division: (1) sequestering negative regulators of division, (2) enriching positive regulators to increase their nuclear concentration, or (3) diffuse nucleoplasmic Oskar acting directly as a cell cycle regulator with granules serving as a protein source.
results.evaluation: Claims C186-C187, C189, C193-C194, C196 are explicitly speculative models proposed by the authors. While these are reasonable hypotheses based on the data and analogies to other systems (e.g., C188), they are not tested in the current study. The presence of cell cycle proteins in the Oskar IP (C190) provides some support for models 1 and 2, but no direct evidence is provided to distinguish among the models or establish mechanism.

results.result: Background on germ granules and phase separation: Germ granules are non-membranous RNP granules linked to germ cell fate across species. They resemble other condensates like P bodies and stress granules. Proteins that phase separate often contain LC domains or IDRs and can form liquid droplets or transition to hydrogel-like states. Drosophila germ granules behave more like aged stress granules than C. elegans P granules.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C10-C22, C132-C133, C215-C220 provide established background knowledge supported by extensive citations. The comparison to other systems (C217-C220) is supported by the biophysical data presented in the current study. This contextualizes the findings appropriately.

results.result: Background on Drosophila PGC formation: Nuclei migrate to the embryo periphery at NC9, and those reaching the posterior become engulfed by germ plasm to form PGCs at NC10. PGCs undergo four divisions before cellularization of somatic cells, then arrest in G2 phase. Nuclear granules appear once PGCs form and are populated by Oskar.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C35, C54-C55, C185 provide established developmental biology background supported by citations. This contextualizes when and how nuclear granules form and sets up the biological significance of the division phenotype.

results.result: RNA and MCM/RuvB-like helicase complexes can stabilize stress granules and promote maturation to hydrogels. Some of these proteins (Mcm5, Mcm3, Dpa, pontin) associate with Short Oskar by IP. RNA can alter biophysical properties of droplets, and mRNA-enriched cytoplasmic germ granules do not fuse, consistent with phase transitioned condensate behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C221-C227 connect observations from other systems to the current findings. The association of MCM/RuvB proteins with Oskar (C222) is supported by citation to previous work. The lack of fusion in mRNA-enriched granules (C225-C226) is supported by current observations and previous work. The inference that these proteins could promote hydrogel-like properties (C223) is reasonable speculation based on analogy to stress granules.

results.result: Nuclear granules have a hollow appearance with an electron-dense shell surrounding a less dense core. Several speculative models are proposed: Oskar forming a shell around other components, phase-separated core with distinct miscible properties, or reentrant phase transition driven by RNA or other charged counterions. The hollow appearance is lost when Oskar's RNA binding domain is deleted.
results.evaluation: Claim C233 describes the morphological observation supported by EM and immunofluorescence. Claims C234-C235, C243, C245 are speculative models. The observation that hollow appearance is lost with ΔSGNH (C244) provides some support for RNA involvement, but the specific mechanism remains unclear. The models are reasonable based on analogies to other systems (C236-C238, C240-C241), but are not directly tested.

results.result: Long Oskar does not form granules in cell lines or embryos despite containing the Short Oskar sequence. The N-terminal extension may fold into helices that solubilize the protein or dictate a fold that makes phase separation motifs inaccessible. The two isoforms are spatially segregated, with Long Oskar enriched cortically and Short Oskar in granules. This separation may prevent granule dissolution by Long Oskar.
results.evaluation: Claim C204 is supported by data in the current study and citations. Claims C205-C206 are speculative mechanisms based on structural predictions. Claims C207-C209 describe established spatial segregation supported by citations. Claim C211 is speculation about the biological significance. While the observations are well-supported, the mechanistic explanations remain speculative.

results.result: Cytoplasmic and nuclear germ granules may use the same biophysical principles to achieve distinct functions. Liquid properties could enhance biochemical reactions or provide diffusible protein, while stable conformation could ensure persistence of regulatory properties throughout development. Cytoplasmic germ granules persist from late oogenesis through early embryogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claim C197 is supported by the biophysical characterization data showing similar properties. Claims C198-C199, C202 are reasonable speculation about functional implications. Claim C200 is supported by citation. Claim C201 is a logical inference. While the functional implications are speculative, they are grounded in the demonstrated biophysical properties.

results.result: Despite years of research, it is unclear how Oskar's distinct functions are accomplished with spatial and temporal precision. Most osk mutations prevent germ plasm assembly during oogenesis, precluding study of later functions. The S2R+ cell system provides an experimentally controllable system to study Oskar properties and functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C212-C213 accurately describe limitations in the field. Claim C214 is supported by the demonstration that S2R+ cells recapitulate key features of nuclear granules. This justifies the use of the cell culture system as a complementary approach to in vivo studies.

results.result: Many granules described as liquid droplets display heterogeneous FRAP behavior with immobile fractions. Examples include CAR-1 in P granules (16% mobile), Dcp2 in P bodies (immobile), and components of stress granules. Protein and RNA composition can influence polymerization and biophysical properties. Non-homogeneous organization with distinct mRNA localization appears to be a hallmark of diverse condensates.
results.evaluation: Claims C228-C232 are supported by citations to previous work and provide context for interpreting the FRAP data. Claims C246-C248 extend this to RNA organization, supported by citations. This contextualizes the findings that Drosophila germ granules have significant immobile fractions and suggests this may be a general feature of functional condensates rather than an exception.

results.result: Test tube experiments provide a useful tool to study phase separation but may not faithfully reflect cellular context. Optimization of the cell culture approach could enable complete functional reconstitution of germ granules in somatic cells, allowing examination of how granule organization specifies germline character.
results.evaluation: Claims C249-C250 are supported by citations and represent a reasonable assessment of the limitations of in vitro approaches. Claims C251-C252 are speculation about future applications of the S2R+ system. While the current study demonstrates that S2R+ cells can recapitulate some features of nuclear granules, complete functional reconstitution has not been achieved and may require additional components.
